A forebear is an ancestor — a person who lived before you in your family, from whom you or your family descended.

Think of your family as a long chain stretching back through time. Every person in that chain who came before you — your parents, grandparents, great-grandparents, their parents, and so on, generation after generation — is your forebear.
Who Exactly Counts as a Forebear?

Technically, even your parents qualify, since they came before you. But in practice, people almost always use "forebear" to refer to distant ancestors — people from several generations ago, often from a different century or era entirely.

You would say:

  • "My forebears came to America from Poland in the 1880s."
  • "Our forebears survived war, drought, and famine."

You would not typically walk up to your mother and call her your forebear. The word carries a sense of distance in time — people you never met, who lived long before you.
Almost Always Used in the Plural

You will encounter this word in its plural form — forebears — the vast majority of the time. This is natural, because ancestors are almost always spoken of as a group: the whole line of people stretching back through history, not a single specific individual.

You can use it in the singular — "She was a forebear of remarkable resilience" — but this is far less common.

"Forebear" is a formal, dignified word. It appears in historical writing, family memoirs, speeches, and literature. It is not a casual, everyday word.

Both "forebear" and "ancestor" mean the same thing. The difference is one of register (the level of formality):

  • In a history book or a speech: "Our forebears sacrificed everything for this country."
  • In casual conversation: "My ancestors were from West Africa."

Using "forebear" signals that you are speaking with gravity and respect — treating the past as something weighty and meaningful.
Can It Be Used Outside of Family?

Yes, occasionally. While "forebear" most commonly refers to literal blood relatives in your family tree, it is sometimes used figuratively to describe the early pioneers of a movement, institution, or field of thought — people who came before and whose work shaped what came after.

For example:

  • "The forebears of modern medicine had no antibiotics to work with."
  • "These architects were the forebears of the entire Modernist movement."

Here, the "family" relationship is replaced by a shared intellectual or historical lineage. The idea is the same: people who came before and passed something important forward.

This figurative use is acceptable and fairly common, but the literal meaning (family ancestor) remains the primary one.

This is perhaps the most important thing to know about this word, because the confusion is extremely widespread — even among native English speakers.

"Forebear" (noun) sounds identical when spoken aloud to "forbear" (verb), but they are completely different words with completely different meanings:

  • forebear (noun) = an ancestor
    • "Her forebears built this town with their bare hands."
  • forbear (verb) = to stop yourself from doing something; to hold back or restrain yourself
    • "He could not forbear from smiling at the absurdity of it."

The spelling is your guide:

  • forebear = "fore" suggests before, as in people who came before you ✓
  • forbear = a verb meaning to hold back ✓

One additional wrinkle worth knowing: some dictionaries do list "forbear" as an alternate spelling of the noun (meaning ancestor), because the two words share the same origin. So you may occasionally see the noun spelled without the 'e'. However, "forebear" is the standard and strongly preferred spelling for the noun, and using it will always be correct and clear.

A forebear is an ancestor — someone who came before you in your family line, typically from a distant, earlier era. It is almost always used in the plural (forebears), carries a formal and respectful tone, and can occasionally be used figuratively to describe the early pioneers of a tradition or field. Its only real pitfall is confusion with the verb forbear (to restrain oneself), which sounds the same but means something entirely different — a distinction you now have no reason to get wrong.
